examinerBank.question: Walk me through your differential diagnosis for this patient's presentation and how the findings point you toward constrictive pericarditis over the alternatives.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: The presentation is right heart failure predominant, with ascites out of proportion to peripheral oedema, a markedly raised JVP with positive Kussmaul's sign, and an impalpable apex with a pericardial knock — this favours constrictive pericarditis over restrictive cardiomyopathy (where the apex would be palpable and myocardium abnormal on echo), over dilated cardiomyopathy (EF is preserved, apex not displaced, no S3), over valvular disease (no murmur), and over primary liver disease (JVP would not be elevated). The history of previously treated pulmonary TB is the strongest risk factor, and pericardial calcification on CXR with pericardial thickening on echo confirms the pericardial origin.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks: ranked differential with reasoning tying each finding to inclusion/exclusion of each diagnosis, explicitly using the apex palpation and Kussmaul's sign as the discriminating features. Partial marks for an unranked list without the constriction-vs-restriction distinction.

examinerBank.question: Explain the pathophysiology of Kussmaul's sign and why it is present in this condition but not in normal physiology or in cardiac tamponade.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Normally inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, increasing venous return to the right heart and causing the JVP to fall. In constrictive pericarditis the rigid, thickened pericardium fixes the total cardiac volume, so the right heart cannot expand to accommodate this increased venous return; venous pressure instead rises paradoxically with inspiration. This differs from tamponade, where the pericardium is under tension from fluid but is not chronically thickened/fibrotic in the same way, and Kussmaul's sign is characteristically absent because the compressive pathology is different (equalisation occurs but without the fixed-volume rigid shell effect on respiration in the same manner).
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants the mechanism of fixed pericardial volume limiting right heart expansion, not just a definition of the sign. Should also attempt the tamponade contrast for higher marks.

examinerBank.question: The echocardiogram shows preserved ejection fraction and pericardial thickening with a septal bounce. How does this change your interpretation compared to if the echo had shown a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: A dilated poorly contracting ventricle would suggest dilated cardiomyopathy (e.g. HIV-related or alcohol-related), requiring standard HFrEF therapy (ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, spironolactone) and addressing the underlying toxin/infection. Instead, preserved EF with pericardial thickening and respirophasic septal shift localises the pathology to the pericardium rather than the myocardium, meaning medical HF therapy alone will not fix the underlying problem — the patient needs surgical pericardiectomy as definitive treatment, and diuretics should be used cautiously since these patients are preload-dependent for maintaining cardiac output.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Tests ability to apply echo findings to change management pathway, specifically recognising that pericardial disease requires surgery rather than standard heart failure pharmacotherapy alone.

examinerBank.question: Before committing this patient to pericardiectomy, what must you actively exclude, and why does it matter?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Active or recent TB pericarditis must be excluded, since an effusive-constrictive phase within the first few months of pericarditis may still respond to anti-tuberculous therapy with corticosteroids and can partially or fully resolve without surgery. This requires repeating sputum/GeneXpert, clinical TB screening, and considering pericardial fluid analysis if an effusion is present. Only once chronic fibrocalcific constriction is confirmed (and reversible/active disease excluded) should the patient proceed to pericardiectomy, since surgery carries significant morbidity and is not warranted if medical therapy could still work.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants recognition of the effusive-constrictive/early reversible phase of TB pericarditis versus chronic fibrocalcific constriction, and that TB status must be reassessed before surgical referral is finalised.

framework: chronic dyspnoea + right heart failure signs → cardiomyopathy vs pericardial disease differentiation

patient.name: Bongani Mthembu
patient.personality: stoic, downplays how limited he has become, gets anxious when asked about his abdomen swelling
patient.openingLine: Doctor, my stomach keeps swelling up and my legs are so tight I can't fit my work boots anymore.

presentingComplaint: progressive abdominal swelling and leg oedema over 3 months with worsening exertional dyspnoea

history.fact: Abdominal swelling and ankle swelling started about 3 months ago and has steadily worsened
Now gets breathless walking to the taxi rank, whereas 6 months ago he could work a full 12-hour shift standing without difficulty
Sleeps propped up on three pillows; used to sleep flat
No episodes of waking up gasping at night
Abdomen has become progressively more distended; belt no longer fits; occasional dull right upper quadrant discomfort
Both legs swell up by the end of the day, worse than a few months ago, pitting, up to the shins
Was treated for pulmonary TB about 2 years ago, completed 6 months of treatment, told he was 'cured'
No current cough, no haemoptysis, no night sweats, no fevers now
No deliberate weight loss noted recently, though clothes feel tighter around the middle from the swelling rather than looser
HIV positive, diagnosed 4 years ago, on ART (tenofovir/lamivudine/dolutegravir), says he takes it 'most days'
Drinks beer socially on weekends, about 4-5 beers on a Saturday, none in the week
No known hypertension or diabetes; no previous heart problems diagnosed
Only takes his ART; no diuretics or other chronic medication currently
Lives in KwaMashu with his wife and two children in a small rented room; works night shifts as a security guard
No family history of heart disease or sudden death; father died of 'old age', mother alive and well
No palpitations, no syncope or presyncope, no chest pain, no haemoptysis, no urinary symptoms, no joint pains

examination.general: Chronically unwell-looking, thin man sitting upright. Mild peripheral cyanosis absent. Visibly distended abdomen. Bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin. No lymphadenopathy. No oral thrush.
examination.respiratory: Reduced air entry at both bases with dullness to percussion suggestive of small bilateral pleural effusions; no crackles higher up; trachea central.
examination.cardio: JVP markedly elevated to the angle of the jaw, with a visible rapid y-descent; JVP rises further on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign positive). Apex beat impalpable/difficult to localise. Heart sounds soft and distant with an early diastolic 'pericardial knock' heard best at the left sternal edge. No murmurs. Pulsus paradoxus not marked.
examination.abdo: Distended, shifting dullness confirming ascites; smooth, pulsatile-feeling hepatomegaly 4 cm below the costal margin, mildly tender; no splenomegaly.
examination.neuro: Alert and orientated, no focal deficit.

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Small bilateral pleural effusions; pericardial calcification visible along the left heart border; heart size not markedly enlarged

investigations.name: Echocardiogram
investigations.result: Thickened, echo-bright pericardium; septal bounce with respirophasic ventricular septal shift; dilated inferior vena cava with minimal respiratory collapse; preserved biventricular systolic function (EF 58%); restrictive mitral inflow pattern with respiratory variation >25%; no significant pericardial effusion

investigations.name: ECG
investigations.result: Low-voltage QRS complexes, non-specific T-wave flattening, no acute ischaemic changes, sinus rhythm

investigations.name: Cardiac CT/MRI
investigations.result: Pericardial thickening measuring 6 mm with patchy calcification, consistent with chronic constrictive pericarditis

investigations.name: HIV test / CD4 count
investigations.result: HIV positive (known), CD4 count 340 cells/µL, viral load suppressed <50 copies/mL on current ART

investigations.name: Urea & electrolytes
investigations.result: Mild hyponatraemia (Na 132 mmol/L) and mildly elevated urea consistent with congestive picture; creatinine normal

investigations.name: Liver function tests
investigations.result: Mildly elevated ALP and GGT with mild hyperbilirubinaemia, in keeping with congestive hepatopathy

investigations.name: NT-proBNP
investigations.result: Mildly elevated (less markedly raised than typically seen in dilated cardiomyopathy of similar severity)

investigations.name: Ascitic tap (diagnostic)
investigations.result: Exudate-range protein, no malignant cells, ADA not significantly elevated (no active TB peritonitis); consistent with cardiac ascites from constriction

investigations.name: Right and left heart catheterisation
investigations.result: Equalisation of end-diastolic pressures across all four chambers; 'dip-and-plateau' (square root sign) in ventricular pressure tracings; discordance between RV and LV systolic pressures with respiration

for: predominant right heart failure signs with ascites out of proportion to peripheral oedema
echo showing pericardial thickening and septal bounce

against: apex beat impalpable rather than easily felt (favours constriction over restriction)
echo shows pericardial thickening rather than myocardial infiltration/granular sparkling
preserved rather than reduced systolic function with normal wall thickness
EF preserved at 58% on echo (DCM expects reduced EF)
JVP y-descent and Kussmaul's sign not typical of DCM

differentials.dx: Rheumatic valvular heart disease (e.g. tricuspid regurgitation)
for: hepatomegaly and ascites can occur with severe TR
against: echo did not describe valvular pathology
pericardial calcification and thickening are the dominant echo findings, not valve disease
no stigmata of chronic liver disease described
JVP is markedly elevated (would be normal/low in isolated liver disease)
Kussmaul's sign and pericardial knock point to a cardiac source

pathophys.Kussmaul's sign (JVP rising on inspirati: The rigid, thickened pericardium prevents the right heart from accommodating the normal inspiratory increase in venous return; instead of falling, right atrial and jugular venous pressure rise as blood dams back into the venous system
pathophys.Ascites out of proportion to peripheral: Chronically elevated systemic venous pressure is transmitted preferentially to the hepatic and splanchnic circulation, causing hepatic congestion and a protein-rich transudate/exudate into the peritoneal cavity before peripheral oedema becomes marked
pathophys.Pericardial knock: Ventricular filling is abruptly halted in early diastole by the non-compliant, thickened pericardial shell once the rigid limit of the sac is reached, producing an early high-pitched diastolic sound (the 'dip' before the 'plateau' seen on catheter tracings)
pathophys.Impalpable/undisplaced apex beat: The thickened, fibrocalcific pericardium encases and dampens transmission of the underlying cardiac impulse to the chest wall, unlike restrictive cardiomyopathy where the myocardium itself is diseased but the pericardium is normal and the apex remains palpable
pathophys.Exertional dyspnoea: Fixed pericardial constriction limits total cardiac filling volume and thus stroke volume/cardiac output cannot rise appropriately with exertion, causing early fatigue and breathlessness despite preserved myocardial contractility
pathophys.Respirophasic septal bounce on echo: Because the total pericardial volume is fixed, an inspiratory increase in right ventricular filling can only occur at the expense of left ventricular volume, causing the interventricular septum to shift abruptly toward the LV in inspiration (ventricular interdependence)

staging: NYHA class III (marked limitation of physical activity); WHO HIV clinical stage 1 (virologically suppressed on ART, CD4 340); constrictive pericarditis presumed post-tuberculous based on prior treated PTB and calcified pericardium (no current active TB)

immediate: Assess volume status and initiate cautious diuresis (loop diuretic e.g. furosemide) to relieve congestion — avoid over-diuresis as filling is preload-dependent
Continue ART uninterrupted; reinforce adherence counselling
Exclude active TB before assuming purely post-inflammatory disease — repeat sputum/GeneXpert and clinical TB screen if any doubt
definitive: Refer for cardiothoracic surgical opinion for pericardiectomy — definitive treatment for symptomatic chronic constrictive pericarditis
If any suspicion of concurrent active TB or recent pericarditis (<2-3 months), consider empirical anti-TB therapy with corticosteroids first, reassess for resolution before committing to surgery
Pre-operative optimisation of nutritional and volume status
Cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery multidisciplinary referral (tertiary centre e.g. Inkosi Albert Luthuli Central Hospital)
supportive: Salt restriction and fluid moderation advice
Nutritional support given cachexia risk pre-surgery
Patient education on chronicity and surgical option, addressing anxiety about prognosis
Home/social support assessment given manual occupation and childcare responsibilities
followUp: Serial weight and abdominal girth monitoring while awaiting surgery
Post-pericardiectomy echo and clinical review to confirm haemodynamic improvement
Continued HIV care — routine CD4/viral load monitoring
Screen household contacts if any suspicion of unresolved/recurrent TB exposure

stationChecklist.item: Introduces self, confirms patient identity, establishes rapport and consent
Confirms this is a heart failure/cardiac presentation before jumping to a specific diagnosis (dyspnoea, oedema, orthopnoea, exercise tolerance)
stationChecklist.answer: Progressive orthopnoea, exertional dyspnoea, leg and abdominal swelling over 3 months
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 1 — must establish the syndrome before naming the cause

stationChecklist.item: Screens for common secondary causes of impaired cardiac function — hypertension, ischaemic symptoms, valvular/rheumatic history
stationChecklist.answer: No hypertension, diabetes, chest pain, or known valve disease
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 2 — hypertensive/ischaemic/valvular disease must be excluded before invoking a less common diagnosis

stationChecklist.item: Specifically asks about previous TB treatment and pericardial/chest TB history
stationChecklist.answer: Treated for pulmonary TB 2 years ago, completed 6 months of therapy
stationChecklist.why: Post-tuberculous constrictive pericarditis is the leading cause of constriction in this setting and the key unifying history point

stationChecklist.item: Asks HIV status, ART regimen and adherence
stationChecklist.answer: HIV positive on TLD, adherence described as 'most days'
stationChecklist.why: HIV status is standard of care in any KZN cardiac presentation and informs risk of recurrent/other opportunistic disease

stationChecklist.item: Screens for alcohol use and other cardiotoxic exposures
stationChecklist.answer: Moderate weekend beer intake, no cocaine/chemotherapy exposure
stationChecklist.why: Excludes alcohol-related dilated cardiomyopathy as an alternative diagnosis

stationChecklist.item: Examines JVP carefully and specifically checks for Kussmaul's sign
stationChecklist.answer: JVP markedly elevated with paradoxical rise on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign positive)
stationChecklist.why: Kussmaul's sign is a hallmark discriminating feature of constrictive physiology

stationChecklist.item: Palpates the apex beat and comments on whether it is displaced/palpable
stationChecklist.why: Distinguishes constrictive pericarditis (impalpable apex due to pericardial encasement) from restrictive cardiomyopathy (apex easily palpable)

stationChecklist.item: Auscultates for a pericardial knock and absence of significant murmurs
stationChecklist.answer: Early diastolic pericardial knock present, no murmurs
stationChecklist.why: Pericardial knock supports constrictive pericarditis over valvular or myocardial disease

stationChecklist.item: Examines abdomen for ascites, hepatomegaly, and assesses degree of peripheral oedema
stationChecklist.answer: Ascites with shifting dullness, tender pulsatile hepatomegaly, bilateral pitting oedema
stationChecklist.why: Demonstrates the right heart failure pattern with ascites disproportionate to peripheral oedema

stationChecklist.item: Generates a ranked differential distinguishing constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy, DCM, valvular disease and liver disease with reasoning
stationChecklist.why: Core symptom-to-differential reasoning required by the exam philosophy — especially the constriction vs restriction distinction

stationChecklist.item: Requests ECG and chest X-ray as first-line tests
stationChecklist.answer: Low-voltage ECG; CXR shows pericardial calcification and small effusions
stationChecklist.why: Initial accessible investigations that raise suspicion of pericardial disease

stationChecklist.item: Requests echocardiogram as the key definitive non-invasive test and interprets findings correctly
stationChecklist.answer: Thickened pericardium, septal bounce, dilated non-collapsing IVC, restrictive mitral inflow with respiratory variation, preserved EF
stationChecklist.why: Echocardiography is the definitive confirmatory investigation per framework step 5

stationChecklist.item: Recognises the role of cardiac catheterisation (equalisation of pressures, dip-and-plateau) when echo is equivocal
stationChecklist.answer: Equalisation of end-diastolic pressures, dip-and-plateau sign
stationChecklist.why: Gold-standard invasive confirmation distinguishing constriction from restriction when non-invasive tests are inconclusive

stationChecklist.item: Identifies pericardiectomy as the definitive treatment and arranges appropriate surgical referral
stationChecklist.answer: Refer for pericardiectomy at a tertiary cardiothoracic centre
stationChecklist.why: Definitive management for symptomatic chronic constrictive pericarditis per guidelines

stationChecklist.item: Outlines cautious diuresis, TB re-exclusion, and ART continuation while awaiting definitive surgery
stationChecklist.answer: Careful diuretic use, screen for active TB before assuming purely fibrotic disease, continue ART
stationChecklist.why: Bridging medical management and safety-netting for reversible active disease
